quiz.q: A service answers a request with 422. Who has to act?
o: The caller: the request was understood and its content is not acceptable
quiz.why: A first digit of 4 blames the request and a 5 blames the service. Repeating a 4xx unchanged is pointless.

quiz.q: Why does the service load the model in the lifespan function and not in the handler?
o: Handlers are not allowed to read files
So that the cost of loading is paid once at start-up and not for every request
Because the model changes between requests
quiz.why: Creating the session took 1.4 ms against 7 microseconds for a prediction. For large models it takes seconds.

quiz.q: You want the runs that have at least 400 events in the Z window. Where does each condition go?
o: The mass window into WHERE, and the count into HAVING
The count into WHERE, and the mass window into HAVING
quiz.why: WHERE filters rows before the grouping. A count exists only after the grouping, so it can only be tested in HAVING.

quiz.q: Why are values put into a query with ? placeholders and never with an f-string?
o: An f-string makes the value part of the SQL text, so whoever supplies the value can change what the query does
quiz.why: That is SQL injection. With a placeholder the database treats the value as a value and nothing else.

quiz.q: A pure-Python loop is run in four threads on four cores. What happens to the run time?
o: It stays about the same or gets slightly worse
Python refuses to start the threads
quiz.why: The global interpreter lock lets one thread at a time run Python code. Processes, or code in NumPy or C++, are the way to use four cores.

quiz.q: A containerised service is started with uvicorn's default host. Why can't it be reached through docker run -p 8000:8000?
o: It listens on 127.0.0.1, which inside a container means the container itself
The image has no EXPOSE line
quiz.why: The port mapping delivers requests to the container's network interface. --host 0.0.0.0 makes the server listen there.

tasks.title: How often does the keep-alive gap bite?
tasks.desc: The last failures of a rollout come from requests that are sent into a connection at the instant its pod closes it. quiz.q: A service is saturated at 1,200 requests per second. A closed-loop test holds 60 connections open. Which latency does Little's law predict?
quiz.why: Requests under way = throughput × latency, so 60 = 1,200 × latency, which gives 0.05 seconds. It is the time spent queueing.

quiz.q: Your single-threaded load generator uses 10 seconds of processor time in a 10-second run. What does its report tell you?
o: The exact capacity of the service
Mostly the limits of the generator itself, so the result must be checked with a faster tool
quiz.why: A generator that is busy all the time measures its own queue. The lesson's generator reported 291 requests per second where ab measured 1,203.

quiz.q: A deployment has 3 replicas, maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0. What happens first in a rolling update?
o: All three old pods are stopped
One new pod is started, and nothing is stopped until it is ready
The service is deleted and created again
quiz.why: No fewer than three may be ready, and one extra is allowed. So the capacity never drops during the update.

quiz.q: What does Kubernetes do with a pod whose readiness probe fails?
o: It stops sending it requests through the service, and leaves it running
It moves it to another node
quiz.why: Restarting is what a failing liveness probe causes. Readiness only decides whether the pod gets traffic.

quiz.q: Why does a pod sleep for a few seconds in a preStop hook before it shuts down?
o: Because its address is removed from the service in parallel, and requests still arrive until that has spread
To give the liveness probe time to fail
quiz.why: Without the pause, requests are routed to a server that has already closed. The lesson measured 11 failed requests without it.

quiz.q: A new release can't start, and its pod shows CrashLoopBackOff. Why do the callers notice nothing?
o: With maxUnavailable 0 no old pod is stopped before a new one is ready, and the new one never is
quiz.why: The old pods keep serving. kubectl logs shows the cause, and kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous version.

quiz.q: How exact is a p99 that Prometheus computes from a histogram?

It is always the upper edge of the last bucket
Exact if the scrape interval is short enough
quiz.why: The histogram only knows how many observations fell into each bucket. Choose the edges around the values you expect.

quiz.q: The handler's histogram reports a p99 of 2.3 ms and the load generator a p99 of 29.9 ms for the same minutes. Why?

quiz.q: An alert rule has for: 30s. The condition has been true for 10 seconds. Which state is the alert in?

quiz.q: You have 2,000 independent files to process, at half an hour each. How do you run that at CERN?

On your laptop over a weekend

quiz.q: Why does an analysis job on the Grid run at the site that holds its data?

drills.title: Reverse the words
drills.prompt:

hints: str.split() with no argument splits on any run of whitespace.

drills.solution:
def reverse_words(s):
    return " ".join(s.split()[::-1])

drills.title: Parse a CSV and sort
drills.prompt: Lines look like "name,energy" (energy is a float). Write read_events(path) that returns a list of (name, energy) tuples sorted by energy, highest first. Skip the header line.
hints: import csv; csv.reader(f) gives lists of strings; next(reader) skips the header.
sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1], reverse=True)
drills.solution:
import csv

def read_events(path):
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        reader = csv.reader(f)

    return out

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_hist(masses, path):
    counts, edges = np.histogram(masses, bins=50, range=(2, 4))

    ax.set_ylabel("Events / 0.04 GeV")

drills.solution:
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

def train_bdt(X, y):
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=42)
    model = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=42)
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    auc_train = roc_auc_score(y_tr, model.predict_proba(X_tr)[:, 1])
    auc_test = roc_auc_score(y_te, model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1])
    return auc_train, auc_test

drills.title: A forward pass by hand
drills.prompt: Write forward(x, W1, b1, W2, b2) for one event, in plain Python. x is a list of inputs. W1 holds one list of weights per hidden neuron and b1 one bias per hidden neuron. W2 and b2 are the same for the output layer. Compute the hidden layer with ReLU, then the logits, and return the softmax probabilities as a list.
hints: One layer is, for each neuron, the sum of weight times input, plus the bias. ReLU is max(z, 0).
Subtract the largest logit before math.exp, so that large logits don't overflow. Then divide by the sum.
drills.solution:
import math

def forward(x, W1, b1, W2, b2):
    hidden = [max(sum(w * xi for w, xi in zip(row, x)) + b, 0.0) for row, b in zip(W1, b1)]
    logits = [sum(w * h for w, h in zip(row, hidden)) + b for row, b in zip(W2, b2)]
    m = max(logits)
    e = [math.exp(z - m) for z in logits]
    s = sum(e)
    return [v / s for v in e]

drills.title: A numerical gradient
drills.prompt: Write numeric_grad(f, w, eps). f is a function that takes a list of numbers and returns one number, and w is a list of numbers. Return a list with, for every position i, the central difference: f with w[i] raised by eps, minus f with w[i] lowered by eps, divided by 2 * eps. The list w itself must not be changed.
hints: Make two copies of w for every position, with list(w), and change one element in each.
The result has the same length as w.
drills.solution:
def numeric_grad(f, w, eps):
    grad = []
    for i in range(len(w)):
        up = list(w)
        down = list(w)
        up[i] += eps
        down[i] -= eps
        grad.append((f(up) - f(down)) / (2 * eps))
    return grad

drills.title: A model as a class
drills.prompt: Write a PyTorch class MLP(nn.Module). Its constructor takes n_in, a list hidden with the sizes of the hidden layers, and n_out. It builds a linear layer followed by a ReLU for every hidden size and a last linear layer without activation. forward returns the logits. Then create MLP(16, [64, 32, 32], 5) and print its number of parameters.
hints: super().__init__() comes first. Collect the layers in a list while you keep track of the size of the previous layer.
nn.Sequential(*layers) turns the list into a model. The star unpacks the list into separate arguments.
drills.solution:
import torch
from torch import nn

class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_in, hidden, n_out):
        super().__init__()
        layers = []
        size = n_in
        for h in hidden:
            layers.append(nn.Linear(size, h))
            layers.append(nn.ReLU())
            size = h
        layers.append(nn.Linear(size, n_out))
        self.net = nn.Sequential(*layers)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)

model = MLP(16, [64, 32, 32], 5)
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))    # 4389

drills.title: One epoch, and an evaluation
drills.prompt: Write train_epoch(model, loader, loss_fn, optimizer): one pass over a DataLoader in training mode, returning the mean training loss per example. Then write evaluate(model, X, y, loss_fn): the loss and the accuracy on the tensors X and y as a tuple of Python numbers, in evaluation mode and without gradients.
hints: The loss of a batch is already a mean over that batch. Multiply it by the batch size before adding it up, and divide by the number of examples at the end.
Compute the logits once in evaluate, and use them for both the loss and the accuracy.
drills.solution:
def train_epoch(model, loader, loss_fn, optimizer):
    model.train()
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    for xb, yb in loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total += loss.item() * len(yb)
        count += len(yb)
    return total / count

def evaluate(model, X, y, loss_fn):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = model(X)
        loss = loss_fn(logits, y).item()
        accuracy = (logits.argmax(dim=1) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss, accuracy

Write three functions. count_between(con, low, high) returns the number of events whose mass lies between low and high, both ends included. heaviest(con, n) returns a list of the n events with the largest mass as (run, event, mass) tuples, heaviest first. count_runs(con) returns the number of different runs. drills.title: GROUP BY, HAVING and a JOIN
drills.prompt: con is an open sqlite3 connection with the tables events(run, event, ..., mass) and runs(run, n_events). Write busy_runs(con, low, high, minimum): for the events with a mass between low and high, the runs that have at least minimum of them, as a list of (run, count) tuples with the largest count first. Then write fractions(con, low, high): for every run, the percentage of its events that lie in the mass window, rounded to two digits, as (run, percent) tuples with the largest percentage first.
hints: The mass window is a condition on rows and goes into WHERE. The minimum is a condition on groups and goes into HAVING COUNT(*) >= ?.
Join events with runs ON e.run = r.run, group by the run, and divide 100.0 * COUNT(*) by r.n_events. The decimal point in 100.0 keeps the division from being an integer division.
drills.solution:
def busy_runs(con, low, high, minimum):
    sql = """SELECT run, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events
             WHERE mass BETWEEN ? AND ?
             GROUP BY run
             HAVING COUNT(*) >= ?
             ORDER BY n DESC"""
    return con.execute(sql, (low, high, minimum)).fetchall()


def fractions(con, low, high):
    sql = """SELECT r.run,
                    ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / r.n_events, 2) AS percent
             FROM events AS e JOIN runs AS r ON e.run = r.run
             WHERE e.mass BETWEEN ? AND ?
             GROUP BY r.run
             ORDER BY percent DESC"""
    return con.execute(sql, (low, high)).fetchall()

drills.title: The core of a load generator
drills.prompt: Write the core of a closed-loop load generator with asyncio and httpx. The coroutine user(client, url, body, deadline, latencies, errors) sends POST requests with the JSON text body until time.perf_counter() passes deadline. It appends the duration of every request that was answered with 200 to the list latencies, and counts everything else in the dictionary errors, under 'status NNN' or under the name of the exception. The coroutine run(url, body, connections, seconds) starts that many users on one shared client and returns the tuple (requests per second, p99 in milliseconds).
hints: Time each request with two calls of time.perf_counter(). Catch httpx.HTTPError around the request, and use type(e).__name__ as the key.
async with httpx.AsyncClient(...) as client, then await asyncio.gather(*[user(...) for _ in range(connections)]). The rate is the number of latencies divided by the elapsed time.
drills.solution:
import asyncio
import time

import httpx
import numpy as np

HEADERS = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}


async def user(client, url, body, deadline, latencies, errors):
    while time.perf_counter() < deadline:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        try:
            r = await client.post(url, content=body, headers=HEADERS)
            if r.status_code == 200:
                latencies.append(time.perf_counter() - start)
            else:
                key = "status %d" % r.status_code
                errors[key] = errors.get(key, 0) + 1
        except httpx.HTTPError as e:
            key = type(e).__name__
            errors[key] = errors.get(key, 0) + 1


async def run(url, body, connections, seconds):
    latencies, errors = [], {}
    limits = httpx.Limits(max_connections=connections)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(limits=limits, timeout=10.0) as client:
        start = time.perf_counter()
        deadline = start + seconds
        await asyncio.gather(*[
            user(client, url, body, deadline, latencies, errors)
            for _ in range(connections)])
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    p99 = float(np.percentile(np.array(latencies) * 1000, 99))
    return len(latencies) / elapsed, p99

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Python, the shell and Git from memory
checkpoints.intro:
This checkpoint answers one question: after four weeks, what can you write without looking anything up? It covers the Python lessons of weeks 1 to 4, the shell, bash scripts and Git.

There are twelve tasks. Five are Python functions that you write here and that are checked by running them. Two are done in your own terminal, and you paste what they print. Five are questions with one answer.

Before you start the clock: open a terminal in an empty folder, and check that `python3 --version` and `git --version` both work there. Then close everything else.

blocks.q: Write `initials(name)`. It returns the first letter of every word in upper case, each followed by a dot. Extra spaces between or around the words must not matter.
blocks.test:
print(initials("ada lovelace"))
print(initials("  marie   sklodowska curie "))
print(initials("x"))
blocks.solution:
def initials(name):
    return "".join(word[0].upper() + "." for word in name.split())
blocks.why: `split()` without an argument splits at any run of whitespace and ignores it at the ends. `join` glues the pieces together.

blocks.q: Write `tally(words)`. It returns a dictionary that maps each word, in lower case, to the number of times it occurs. `Mu` and `mu` count as the same word.
blocks.test:
print(sorted(tally(["Mu", "e", "mu", "E", "tau"]).items()))
print(tally([]))
blocks.why: The counting pattern: `counts.get(key, 0) + 1` reads the old count, or 0 for a word seen for the first time.

blocks.q: Write a class `Bin` for one bin of a histogram. `Bin(low, high)` stores the two edges and starts with a count of 0. `fill()` adds one to the count. `width()` returns high minus low. Printing a bin with edges 2.0 and 3.0 and a count of 2 must give `Bin(2.0, 3.0: 2)`, also when the bin is inside a list.
blocks.test:
b = Bin(2.0, 3.0)
b.fill()
b.fill()
print(b)
print(b.width())
print([Bin(0, 1)])
blocks.why: Inside a list, Python shows each element with `__repr__`. A class that defines only `__str__` would fail the last line.

blocks.q: Write a generator function `pairs(items)`. It yields every pair `(items[i], items[j])` with i smaller than j, as a tuple, in order of i and then j. Use `yield`.
blocks.test:
print(list(pairs(["a", "b", "c"])))
print(len(list(pairs(list(range(10))))))
print(next(pairs([1, 2, 3])))
print(list(pairs([])))
blocks.why: Starting the inner loop at `i + 1` gives each pair once. This is the loop behind "every pair of muons in the event". The third line of the check calls `next`, which works only on a generator.

blocks.q: Write `clean(values)`. It takes a list of strings and returns a tuple: the list of those that could be converted to `float`, in order, and the number of strings that could not.
blocks.test:
print(clean(["1.5", "abc", "2", "", "-3e2"]))
print(clean([]))
blocks.why: `float` raises `ValueError` for text that isn't a number, the empty string included. Catching exactly that exception, and counting what you skip, is how real data is read.

blocks.q:
```
import numpy as np

a = np.array([4, 12, 7, 20, 3, 17])
print(a[a > 6].sum(), (a > 6).sum())
```
blocks.why: `a > 6` is a mask of True and False. Indexing with it keeps 12, 7, 20 and 17, which add up to 56. Summing the mask itself counts the True values: 4.

blocks.q:
```
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = a[:]
b.append(4)
s = "invariant mass"
print(len(a), len(c), s[-4:], s.split()[0][:3])
```
blocks.why: `b` is a second name for the same list, so the append is visible through `a`. `c` is a copy made before the append. `s[-4:]` is the last four characters, and `s.split()[0][:3]` is the first three characters of the first word.

blocks.q:
What does this pipeline print?
```
printf 'b
a
b
c
b
' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1
```
blocks.why: `sort` brings equal lines together, `uniq -c` collapses them with a count in front, `sort -rn` puts the largest count first, and `head -n 1` keeps that line.

blocks.q:
Write a bash script `count.sh`. It takes a directory as its first argument, with the current directory as the default. It prints the number of files ending in `.csv` in that directory and everything below it, in the form `3 csv files`. If the directory doesn't exist, it prints a message and exits with code 1. Then run these three commands and paste the output.
```
mkdir -p t/sub && touch t/a.csv t/b.csv t/c.txt t/sub/d.csv
./count.sh t
./count.sh nothere; echo "exit $?"
```
blocks.why: The pieces: a default for the argument with `${1:-.}`, a directory test with `[[ -d ... ]]`, `find` with a quoted pattern, `$( )` to capture a count, and `exit 1` for the failure. Don't forget `chmod +x count.sh`.

blocks.q: A commit that you pushed to the shared `main` branch yesterday turns out to be wrong. Others have already pulled it. How do you undo it?
options: `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, followed by a forced push
`git revert` with the commit's id, which adds a new commit that undoes the change
`git restore .`
Delete the repository and create it again
blocks.why: History that others already have must not be rewritten. `git revert` leaves the old commit in place and records the undo as a new commit that everyone can pull.

blocks.q: You run `git add notes.txt`, then edit `notes.txt` again, then run `git commit -m "Update notes"`. What does the commit contain?
options: The latest version of the file
The version of the file as it was when you ran `git add`
Both versions
Nothing, because the file changed after it was staged
blocks.why: `git add` copies the file's current state into the staging area, and a commit records the staging area. The later edit is still an unstaged change in your working folder.

blocks.q:
In a new, empty folder: create a repository and commit a file. Create a branch called `feature`, switch to it, and commit a change there. Switch back to the first branch and commit a change to a different file. Merge `feature` into it. Then paste the output of the command below.
```
git log --oneline --graph --all
```
blocks.why: Because both branches have a commit of their own, Git can't fast-forward and creates a merge commit with two parents. In the graph you see the two lines split and join again.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 2: C++ and physics from memory
checkpoints.intro:
This checkpoint covers the C++ of weeks 1 to 8 and the physics lessons. There are fourteen tasks.

Three are complete C++ programs. You write each one from an empty file on your own machine, compile it with `g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra`, run it, and paste what it prints. Give them most of your time: about fifteen minutes each. The other eleven are questions with one answer, and you get one attempt at each.

Before you start the clock: open a terminal in an empty folder and an editor with autocompletion from AI switched off. Check that `g++ --version` works. Then close everything else.

blocks.q:
Write `numbers.cpp`. The program takes a file name on the command line and reads whole numbers from that file until it ends. It prints three lines: `evens` followed by how many of the numbers are even, `max` followed by the largest, and then the distinct values in ascending order, separated by spaces. If the file can't be opened, it prints a message to `std::cerr` and returns 1. Compile it to `numbers`, run the three commands and paste the output.
```
printf '5 3 8 3 10 5 1\n' > nums.txt
./numbers nums.txt
./numbers nothere.txt; echo "exit $?"
```
blocks.why: The parts: `argc` and `argv`, an `ifstream` that is checked, the read loop `while (in >> x)`, and `std::sort`. After sorting, the largest value is at the back and equal values are neighbours, so skipping a value equal to the one before it leaves the distinct ones. A `std::map` or `std::set` works too.

blocks.q: Write `hist.cpp` with a class `Histogram`. Its constructor takes the number of bins and the lower and upper edge. `fill(x)` adds one to the right bin. A value below the range counts as underflow, and a value at or above the upper edge as overflow. In `main`, make a histogram with 10 bins from 0 to 10, fill it with 0.5, 1.2, 1.9, 9.99, -1.0 and 10.0, and print the ten bin counts on one line and `underflow U overflow O` on the next. Paste the output.
blocks.why: The bin number is the distance from the lower edge, divided by the width of the range, times the number of bins, cut down to a whole number. Checking the two edges first keeps that index inside the vector. Private data with a trailing underscore, a constructor with an initialiser list, and `const` on the function that only reads.

blocks.q: Write `mass.cpp` with a struct `FourVector` that holds E, px, py and pz, has an `operator+` and a function `mass()`. In `main`, print three masses, one per line: of the sum of (45.6, 45.6, 0, 0) and (45.6, -45.6, 0, 0), of the sum of (50, 30, 0, 40) and (50, -30, 0, -40), and of the single vector (50, 30, 0, 40). The numbers are E, px, py, pz in GeV. Paste the output.
blocks.why: The three lines are 91.2, 100 and 0. In the first two pairs the momenta cancel, so the mass is the sum of the energies. The single vector has E equal to the size of its momentum, which makes it massless.
`by_value` changes its own copy, so `a` stays 1. `by_ref` works on `a` itself: 11. `by_ptr` receives the address of `a` and changes what is stored there: 101.
Through a reference, the virtual call finds the `Circle` version at run time. Passing by value copies only the `Shape` part of the object, which is called slicing, and the copy really is a `Shape`.
Strings compare alphabetically, and "tau" comes after "mu". For the last call T is `int`, so the result 7 is an `int`, and 7 / 2 is integer division: 3.

blocks.q: A class allocates an array with `new` in its constructor and frees it with `delete[]` in its destructor. What else must it define before objects of it can be copied safely?
options: Nothing. The compiler generates correct copies
A default constructor
A copy constructor and a copy assignment operator, because the generated ones copy only the pointer, and two objects would then free the same memory
A virtual destructor
blocks.why: This is the rule of three: a class that needs its own destructor almost always needs its own copy constructor and copy assignment too. Better still, hold a `std::vector` and need none of them.

blocks.q: In a `CMakeLists.txt`, what does `target_link_libraries(app PRIVATE stats)` do?
options: It builds the library `stats` from the sources of `app`
It makes the program `app` use the library `stats`: the library is linked in, and `app` gets the include folders that `stats` declared as PUBLIC
It installs `stats` on the system
It runs the tests of `stats` before building `app`
blocks.why: Linking a target passes on its public properties, which is why `app` finds the library's headers without any further line.

blocks.q: A loop reads `v[v.size()]` once, one element past the end of a vector, and the program still prints the right result. Which statement is true?
options: The code is correct, because the output is correct
`std::vector` checks every index, so nothing was read
It is undefined behaviour that happened to do no visible harm this time. Building with `-fsanitize=address` would report it
The compiler would have refused to compile it if it were wrong
blocks.why: Reading past the end is not checked by `[]`. Whatever lies behind the vector is read, and the result can change with the compiler, the flags or the day.

blocks.q: Which part of a detector such as ATLAS or CMS measures the energy of electrons and photons?
options: The tracker
The electromagnetic calorimeter
The hadronic calorimeter
The muon chambers
blocks.why: Electrons and photons shower and stop in the electromagnetic calorimeter. The tracker measures the paths of charged particles and doesn't see photons at all.

blocks.q: You count 10,000 events in a peak. What is the relative statistical uncertainty of that number?
blocks.why: The uncertainty of a count is √N, here 100, and 100 / 10,000 is 1%. For 0.1% you would need a hundred times more events.

blocks.q: A fit returns χ²/ndf = 1.1. What does that tell you?
options: The fit failed
The fitted parameters are wrong by 10%
The model describes the data about as well as the error bars allow
The uncertainties are 1.1 times too small
blocks.why: On average each point contributes about 1 to χ² when the model is right and the uncertainties are realistic. Values far above 1 point to a wrong model, and values far below 1 to overestimated errors.

blocks.q: Two photons fly apart back to back, each with an energy of 62.5 GeV. What is their invariant mass in GeV?
blocks.why: Photons are massless and the momenta cancel, so the mass is the sum of the energies. This is how the Higgs boson shows up in its decay to two photons.

blocks.q: A process has a cross-section of 50 pb. How many events of it are produced in 20 fb⁻¹ of collisions? Type the number.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 3: fast C++ from memory
checkpoints.intro:
This checkpoint covers weeks 11 to 14: move semantics, memory layout, modern C++, profiling, vectorisation, threads and OpenMP. There are fifteen tasks.

Four are complete programs. You write each from an empty file on your own machine, compile it, run it and paste what it prints. Plan about fifteen minutes for each. The other eleven are questions with one answer, and you get one attempt at each.

Before you start the clock: open a terminal in an empty folder and an editor with AI autocompletion switched off. Check that `g++ --version` works and that a file with `#include <omp.h>` compiles with `-fopenmp`. Then close everything else. No notes, no search, no AI.

blocks.why: `a` and `b` were moved from, so both report 0. `c` took the five elements of `a`, and `d` took the copy that `b` had made of `c`. Any double delete or leak would have made the sanitizers speak.

`push_back(h)` copies a named object. With `std::move` it moves. `emplace_back()` builds the element in place, so nothing is printed. `Hit{}` is a temporary, which is moved in. The `reserve` prevents any reallocation.
In `S` each char is followed by seven bytes of padding. In `R` the two chars share the eight bytes after the double.

blocks.q: Summing ten million integers takes several times longer in a `std::list` than in a `std::vector`. What is the main reason?
options: The list has a worse complexity
The list's elements are scattered heap blocks reached through pointers, so most steps miss the cache
The list is not optimised at `-O2`
The vector uses several threads
blocks.why: Both are linear. A vector's elements share cache lines and can be prefetched.

blocks.q:
Write `fields.cpp`. It takes a file name on the command line. Each line of the file holds fields separated by commas. For every line, the program adds up the fields that are numbers and counts the fields that are not, and prints `sum S bad B`. Split the line with `std::string_view` and parse with `std::from_chars`, without creating a `std::string` per field. If the file can't be opened, print a message to `std::cerr` and return 1. Compile with `-std=c++20`, run these commands and paste the output.
```
printf '1.5,2.5,x,4\n10,,0.25\n7\n' > rows.txt
./fields rows.txt
./fields nothere.txt; echo "exit $?"
```
blocks.why: The empty field between the two commas of the second line is not a number, so it counts as bad.

blocks.q: What does the report line `missed: not vectorized: control flow in loop` usually mean for a loop that only calls `std::sqrt`?
options: The loop has too many iterations
`sqrt` must set `errno` for negative input, which needs a hidden branch. `-fno-math-errno` removes it
The array is not aligned
`-march=native` is missing
blocks.why: Without `-march=native` the loop would still vectorise, with narrower registers.

blocks.q: An event is stored as eight floats. How many megabytes are five million events? Use 1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes.
blocks.why: 8 × 4 = 32 bytes per event, times 5,000,000.

blocks.q: Write `sevens.cpp`. Four threads made with `std::thread` count the multiples of 7 among the whole numbers from 0 to 99,999,999, each in its own quarter of the range. Use no mutex and no atomic. The program prints `multiples` followed by the total. Compile with `g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -pthread sevens.cpp -o sevens` and paste the output.
blocks.why: Each thread counts in a local variable and writes one result into its own slot. Zero counts as a multiple of 7, which is where the final 5 comes from.

blocks.q: Which situation is a data race?
options: Four threads read the same `const std::vector<double>`
Four threads each fill their own histogram
Four threads call `fill` on the same histogram with no lock
Four threads add to the same `std::atomic<long>`
blocks.why: A shared object, writers, and nothing that coordinates them. Reading together is safe, private data is safe, and an atomic coordinates by itself.

blocks.q: 80% of a program's run time can be spread over cores, and 20% can't. What is its speed-up on 4 cores, by Amdahl's law? Give one decimal.

Write `squares.cpp`. For every whole number `i` from 0 to 9,999,999 it computes `(i * i) % 7` and counts how often each of the seven possible results occurs, in an array `long counts[7]`. Parallelise the loop with OpenMP so that there is no data race, and print the seven counts on one line. Compile with `g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -fopenmp squares.cpp -o squares` and paste the output.
blocks.why: The array reduction gives each thread its own seven counters. Squares only ever leave the remainders 0, 1, 2 and 4 when divided by 7, which is why three counts are zero.

blocks.q: Four threads each increment their own `std::atomic<long>` in a small array, and the program is ten times slower than expected. What is the cause and the cure?
options: A data race. Add a mutex
False sharing: the counters lie on one cache line. Pad them with `alignas(64)` or count in local variables
Too many threads. Use two
Atomics are slow. Use `volatile`
blocks.why: The variables are different, but the cache line is shared, and every write takes it away from the other cores.

blocks.q: A job takes 20 s on one thread and 4 s on eight. Type the speed-up and the efficiency in percent.
Four threads fill histograms from 20 million events. Which design is correct and scales best?
options: One shared histogram, no protection
One shared histogram, a mutex around every `fill`
One histogram per thread, added together after the threads have joined
One shared histogram of `volatile long`
blocks.why: Private data needs no locking, and the merge happens once per thread.

blocks.q: In ROOT's RDataFrame, when does the event loop run?
options: When `Filter` is called
When `Histo1D` is called
When the first result is requested, for example with `GetValue()`. It then fills everything booked so far
When the script ends
blocks.why: Filters, definitions and actions are only booked. This is lazy evaluation.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 4: networks, services and contributions from memory
checkpoints.intro:
This is the last checkpoint. It covers weeks 15 to 21: neural networks and PyTorch, quantisation and ONNX, web services, SQL, asyncio, Kubernetes, metrics, reading code and the pull request workflow. There are sixteen tasks.

Five are complete programs or files. You write each from an empty file on your own machine, run it and paste what it prints. Plan about fifteen minutes for each. The other eleven are questions with one answer, and you get one attempt at each.

Before you start the clock: open a terminal in an empty folder and an editor with AI autocompletion switched off. Check that `python -c "import torch, fastapi, httpx"` prints nothing, and that `kubectl get nodes` shows the node of your kind cluster as `Ready`. Create the cluster first if it is gone. Then close everything else. No notes, no search, no AI.

blocks.q: Write `fit.py`. Make 100 points with `x` evenly spaced from -1 to 1 and `y = 2 * x + 1`, as tensors of shape (100, 1). Fit them with one `nn.Linear(1, 1)`, the mean squared error and SGD with a learning rate of 0.1, for 500 steps on all points at once. Print the weight and the bias with two decimals, separated by a space. Paste the output.
blocks.why: The four lines inside the loop are the whole of training: clear the old gradients, compute the loss, compute the gradients, take the step. The data has no noise, so the fit recovers the slope 2 and the offset 1 exactly, whatever the random start was.

blocks.q: A network with two classes gives the logits 0 and 0 for an event. What is the cross-entropy loss for that event? Give three decimals.
blocks.why: The softmax of two equal logits is 0.5 for each class, and the loss is the negative logarithm of the probability of the true class: -ln 0.5 = 0.693. It is the loss of a network that knows nothing about two classes, and a useful number to recognise at the start of a training.

blocks.q: In which order do the four steps of one training iteration in PyTorch come?
options: `optimizer.step()`, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.zero_grad()`, compute the loss
`optimizer.zero_grad()`, compute the loss, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`
compute the loss, `optimizer.step()`, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.zero_grad()`
`loss.backward()`, `optimizer.zero_grad()`, compute the loss, `optimizer.step()`
blocks.why: The gradients must be cleared before `backward` adds the new ones, `backward` needs a loss, and `step` needs the gradients.

blocks.q: What is the step between two neighbouring values of the fixed-point type `ap_fixed<8, 3>`? Give a decimal number.
blocks.why: Of the 8 bits, 3 stand before the point, the sign included, and 5 after it. The step is 2 to the power -5, which is 1/32.

blocks.q: You export a model to ONNX. On the same inputs, the outputs of PyTorch and of ONNX Runtime differ by 2e-7 at most. What do you conclude?
options: The export is broken, because the outputs must be identical
ONNX Runtime uses 16-bit numbers
The export is fine. The two engines add the same numbers in a different order, and float32 arithmetic then differs in the seventh digit
The model was quantised during the export
blocks.why: A float32 has about seven significant digits, and the order of additions changes the rounding. A difference of 1e-2 would be a bug, usually a preprocessing step that was applied twice or not at all.

blocks.q:
Write `service.py`: a FastAPI application with `GET /healthz`, which returns the JSON object with the key `status` and the value `ok`, and `POST /square`, which takes a JSON body with a number under the key `x` and returns the square under the key `y`. Put the lines below at the end of the file, run it with `python service.py` and paste the output.
```
if __name__ == "__main__":
    from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
    client = TestClient(app)
    r = client.get("/healthz")
    print(r.status_code, r.json())
    r = client.post("/square", json={"x": 3})
    print(r.status_code, r.json())
    print(client.post("/square", json={"x": "three"}).status_code)
    print(client.get("/square").status_code)
    print(client.get("/nothing").status_code)
```
blocks.why: The last three status codes come without a line of your own code. The pydantic model rejects a body whose `x` is not a number with 422, a path that exists only for POST answers a GET with 405, and an unknown path gives 404.

blocks.q: `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` prints `SCAN events` for a query that filters on the column `run`. What does that mean, and what is the usual cure?
options: The query is wrong and returns no rows. Rewrite the `WHERE` clause
Every row of the table is read. Create an index on `run`, after which the plan says `SEARCH ... USING INDEX`
The table is locked by another connection. Wait and try again
The database file is damaged. Restore it from a backup
blocks.why: Without an index the database has no choice but to look at every row. With one it goes straight to the matching rows, and the cost grows with the logarithm of the table size.

blocks.q:
Write `failed.py`. It creates an SQLite database in memory with a table `jobs (site TEXT, status TEXT, seconds REAL)`, inserts the rows below with placeholders, and prints one line for every site that has at least two failed jobs: the site, the number of its failed jobs and their mean duration rounded to one decimal. The site with the most failed jobs comes first. Let the database do the counting, with one query. Paste the output.
```
rows = [
    ("CERN", "done", 310.0), ("CERN", "failed", 12.0),
    ("CERN", "done", 290.0), ("FNAL", "failed", 8.0),
    ("FNAL", "failed", 15.0), ("FNAL", "done", 400.0),
    ("KIT", "done", 350.0), ("KIT", "failed", 20.0),
    ("KIT", "failed", 30.0), ("KIT", "failed", 10.0),
]
```
blocks.why: `WHERE` chooses the rows before the grouping and `HAVING` chooses the groups after it. CERN has one failed job and drops out at `HAVING`. The question marks are placeholders, which keep the values apart from the text of the query.

blocks.q: A handler is written with `async def` and calls `time.sleep(1)` inside. What happens to the other requests during that second?
options: Nothing. Each request has its own thread
They are answered with status 503
They all wait, because the handler blocks the event loop on which every coroutine runs
They are moved to another process
blocks.why: An `async def` handler runs on the event loop itself and must await everything slow. `time.sleep` does not give the loop back. Either use `await asyncio.sleep(1)`, or write the handler with `def`, so that it runs in a worker thread.

blocks.q: Write `limit.py`. Ten coroutines `work(i)` each wait 0.05 seconds with `asyncio.sleep` and return `i * i`. At most three of them may be in the waiting part at the same time. Count how many are in it, remember the largest count that ever occurs, run all ten together and print that largest count and the sum of the ten results. Paste the output.
blocks.why: The semaphore lets three coroutines in and makes the others wait at `async with`. The counters need no lock: only one coroutine runs at a time, and it can be interrupted only at an `await`.

blocks.q: A client sends a GET request to a path that the service offers only for POST. Which status code does it get?
blocks.why: 405 Method Not Allowed: the path exists, but not for this method. A path that does not exist at all gives 404.

blocks.q: A deployment has 5 replicas, `maxSurge: 2` and `maxUnavailable: 1`. During a rolling update, what is the largest number of its pods that can exist at the same time, and what is the smallest number that must be ready? Type two numbers.
blocks.why: The surge allows two pods more than the five that are wanted, and at most one of the five may be missing.

blocks.q:
Write `deploy.yaml`: a Deployment with the name `x4-echo` and 3 replicas of the image `jet-service:0.2`. The pods carry the label `app: x4-echo`, and the container listens on port 8000. Add a readiness probe that sends a GET to `/readyz` on that port, a CPU request of a quarter of a core, and a rolling update that never has fewer than three ready pods and at most one more than three. Run the commands below and paste the output of both.
```
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml
C='.spec.template.spec.containers[0]'
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml -o jsonpath="{.spec.replicas} \
{.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable} \
{$C.readinessProbe.httpGet.path} {$C.resources.requests.cpu}"
```
blocks.why: A server dry run sends the file to the cluster, which checks it completely and creates nothing. A misspelt field is refused with `unknown field`. The second command prints four of the values that you wrote. The selector must match the labels of the pod template, or the server rejects the Deployment.

blocks.q: The counter `requests_total` of a service reads 1200. One minute later it reads 1500. What does `rate(requests_total[1m])` show for that minute?
blocks.why: `rate` gives the increase per second: 300 requests in 60 seconds. A counter only ever grows, so its raw value says little. Its rate is what you plot and alert on.

blocks.q: You are reading a codebase that is built on a framework. A method `configure_optimizers` is defined in a class, and `git grep` finds no call of it anywhere in the repository. What does that tell you?
options: The method is dead code
The search is broken, because every method has a caller
The framework calls it. The class inherits from a framework class whose contract prescribes that method name
It is called from a configuration file
blocks.why: This is inversion of control: you write the method, and the framework calls it at the right moment. To learn when, read the framework's documentation for the base class.

blocks.q: You rebased the branch of your own pull request onto `upstream/main`. A plain `git push` is rejected as non-fast-forward. What is the right command?
options: `git pull`, as the hint of Git suggests
`git push --force origin main`
`git push --force-with-lease`
`git reset --hard origin/main`
blocks.why: The rebase wrote new commits, and they must replace the old ones on your fork. The lease form does that only if nobody else has pushed to the branch since your last fetch. `git pull` would merge the old copies back in, and `main` is never force-pushed.

pages.note: **Check the date on CERN's own page.** The 21 January date comes from the 2027 job listings. The official openlab page didn't show a date yet when this plan was made, and its apply link still pointed at 2026. Confirm on the [CERN careers portal](https://careers.cern/) and the [openlab page](https://openlab.cern/cern-openlab-summer-student-programme) before you submit.
pages.intro: Both calls ask for a CV, one academic reference letter less than 12 months old, your latest official transcript and an enrolment certificate, as clearly labelled PDFs in English or French. You upload the reference letter yourself, so ask early. For openlab a motivation letter is recommended, not required. Write one anyway and name the area you want.
